newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Coast Guard working to keep Mississippi open.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Coast Guard working to keep Mississippi open.

text.p: The U.S. Coast Guard plans to keep the Mississippi River open as long as shipping traffic can navigate safely on the flood-swollen river, a Coast Guard spokesman said on Wednesday.
"Our intention right now is as long as we can keep it open safely, that's what we are going to do," said Coast Guard Chief Warrant Officer Chris Haley.

Officials with the Coast Guard, which has authority over commercial shipping on the river, met with Louisiana Gov. Mike Foster on Tuesday to discuss his concerns about a spate of recent barge and freighter accidents.
A spokesman with Gov. Foster's office said he was not pushing the Coast Guard to shut the waterway, one of several rumors that floated through commodities markets yesterday.

A U.S. Army Corps of Engineers chief engineer in New Orleans said there also are no plans to open the Morganza Spillway upriver from Baton Rouge to divert water through the Atchafalaya Basin and Atchafalaya River to the Gulf of Mexico.
A series of public notices would be required before the spillway could be opened, he said.

Officials also said a blue haze seen floating over sections of the river consisted of a mist that trapped exhaust fumes, and was not a lethal chemical release from a capsized barge -- another rumor that wafted through the markets Tuesday.

Crews on Wednesday were rigging up a crane to right a capsized barge at Baton Rouge that was lightered of its cargo of a benzene-laden gasoline. That stretch of the river could be reopened on Thursday once the barge is moved, Haley said.
"Once we get it turned back over, they will stabilize it and move it to a shipyard," he said.
The Mississippi river is expected to crest Saturday morning at Baton Rouge at 44 feet, the height of the lowest part of a levee downtown where a 3-foot deep sandbag wall has been erected.
Shipping along the river was slowed Wednesday morning by thick fog that was slowly burning off. "We're going crazy right now," said a New Orleans pilots dispatcher.
